title: The many faces of Skanda
description: From Devanagari to Unicode: why Skanda is more than a domain name.

body:
# The many faces of Skanda

No important name has only one face. **Skanda** appears as a ​figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in turn: ‌the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in a browser. ‌Taken together, those faces explain why *skanda* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Skanda
- ​**ASCII form:** skanda
- **Meaning:** "‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods."
- **Domain ​of influence:** War, Commander
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** स्कन्द (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Skanda** (*skanda*) — War, the Divine Hosts · ‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva ​— belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "War, Commander". The name means "‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god ​of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods.".

**Skanda** is the Hindu war-god: the ever-youthful general of the devas’ hosts, born from the combined fire of Śiva’s ​third eye to destroy the demon Tāraka. Tamil India knows him as Murugan, the eternally beautiful mountain lord of the six abodes; the Sanskrit world as Kārttikeya, son of the Pleiades’ fosterage.

PuniCodex ‌restores the name as **Skanda** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/skanda/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *skanda* survives as ​a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **स्कन्द**. ​Etymologically it means "‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods.".

The ‌ASCII form *skanda* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Skanda** recovers the full diacritic detail of ​the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **s** → **S** — Same, capitalized
- **k** ‌→ **k** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari ​as **स्कन्द**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Skanda*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Skanda is written in Devanagari as स्कन्द
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin ‌equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈskʌndə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Skanda).

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Skan-** — The cluster sk is preserved; short a as in “cup”.
- **-da** — The name means “the Attacker”, “the Leaper” — a war-name, not a birth-name.
- **-n-** — The cluster ​sk is preserved in every period of the language; no sound is lost between the s and the k.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “SKUN-duh”

Kindred and historical forms of ​the name:

- **Form** — Kārttikeya
- **Form** — Murugan
- **Form** — Subrahmaṇya
- **Kumāra** — (all the same god)
- **Tamil** — Murukan

One god, six names per tradition — born of six sparks from ​the gods’ outraged eyes.

## Mythology

The Skanda myth is the war-god’s birth-saga: the gods, unable to defeat Tāraka, whose boon made him unkillable except by a son of Śiva, contrived the god’s marriage ​to Pārvatī; the child was born as fire from the third eye, fostered by the Pleiades, and general of heaven before he was a week old. The Tamil Murugan traditions add the ‌wooing of Vaḷḷi, the huntress, and the gnostic doctrine of the *Arupadaiveedu*, the six stations of grace.

### The Birth of Fire (Kumāra Cycle)

When Agni and the river Ganges could not carry the ​god’s seed, they left it in the reeds of the Gangā’s bank; six infants were found there by the six Kṛttikā nymphs, each nursing one — until Pārvatī gathered them into a single ‌six-headed child. His first week closed with the death of Tāraka, slain by the spear his mother gave him.

### The Deva-Senāpati (Skanda Purāṇa)

The great Purāṇa bearing his name makes him general ​of the gods’ hosts and husband of Devasenā — ‘the army of the gods’ — a marriage arranged before his birth. His camp is on the world’s margin; his peacock mount, the demon ‌Siṃhakeśin subdued, struts beneath his banner.

### Vaḷḷi and Teyvāyāṉai (Murugan Cycle)

The Tamil epics tell how Murugan wooed the huntress Vaḷḷi in the guise of a tree-shade, and wed both her and ​Teyvāyāṉai, Indra’s daughter, in the great marriage at Tiruchendur. The legend’s two wives read theologically: divine grace (Teyvāyāṉai) and the soul’s own effort (Vaḷḷi) are both needed for union with the lord.

### The ‌Sage-Child (Subrahmaṇya Cycle)

As Subrahmaṇya — ‘the dear one to the Brahmins’ — he is the teacher-god, expounding the Vedas to his own father Śiva in the role of guru. The image ​flips the war-god into wisdom’s child, and fixes his southern temples as places of learning as much as of arms.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Skanda concentrates in a small set ‌of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Divine General** — Commander of the gods’ armies — the deva-senāpati — before whom no asura line holds.
- **Born of the ​Third Eye** — Six sparks from the gods’ wrath-eyes, fostered by the Kṛttikā — the Pleiades — as six infants, fused into one.
- **The Spear** — Śakti, the lance his mother Umā gave ​him — one throw ended Tāraka, the boon-armed demon.
- **Lord of the Six Abodes** — Murugan’s six mountain shrines from Tirupparankunram to Palani mark his Tamil country.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material ‌record for Skanda survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

The six ‌abodes (Ārupadaiveṭṭu) of Tamil Nadu are his living monuments; Gupta and Kushan sculpture give him his classical six-headed infant form. The Batu Caves of Malaysia, a modern Murugan shrine of cathedral scale, ‌extend his geography into the diaspora.

## Realm & Domain

## Across Cultures

Skanda is the great pan-Indian convergence: Vedic Rudra’s son, Tamil Murugan, Buddhist Kārttikeya of the north, and the Graha of the week’s Tuesday. ​The Greeks of the Northwest compared him to Ares and Mars; the Kushan coins show him as Skanda-Kumāra beside the Buddha. His peacock entered Christian art’s immortality symbolism by the strangest of ‌roads.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

Murugan is Tamil country’s beloved god — the Kanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival at ​Tiruchendur draws millions, and the god’s hill-shrines anchor Tamil sacred geography. His six-headed infant image, the Kārttikeya of Gupta art, defined the war-god’s iconography for Asia; and the Ṣaṣṭhī vow is observed ​across the subcontinent by parents of sons.

## A Meditation

Skanda: the war-name that means ‘the one who attacks’. In plain letters it reads like what it is — a battle-cry reduced to a name. ‌The Tamil country still shouts it in festival; the lexicon keeps it here, at rest, its spear laid across the threshold of the temple.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. ​In the case of **Skanda**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form ​*skanda* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script ​attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is ‌romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **s**, **k**, **a**, **n**, **d**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and ​what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Skanda in Its Tradition

**Skanda** does not stand alone. It ​belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is counted among 102 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — War, Commander — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. ​The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Skanda**, it marks ‌the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: ​the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Skanda** is one such vote.

## The Restoration ‌on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Skanda** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the ​public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status ‌of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public web flattened it to *skanda*. Now the public web can carry the correct form ​end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of ‌every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Skanda**, the chain begins ‌with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, ​son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods." anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks ​would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Skanda** and the ASCII form *skanda* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than a ​recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Skanda aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is mechanical, not editorial, which ​means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because every step is recorded ‌in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
